MLT.name: Malta
MLT.summary:
Malta is among the safest countries in the world for transgender visitors. It has ranked first in Europe for LGBTI legal rights every year since 2015: gender identity and expression are protected from discrimination in law, legal gender recognition works by self-determination, and "X" gender markers are available on passports. Conversion therapy is banned and the constitution guarantees LGBTI equality.

Malta records one of the lowest rates of physical or sexual victimisation of LGBTIQ+ people in the EU, and the national police force has adopted hate-crime procedures for SOGIE incidents. The US State Department describes Malta as a safe environment for foreign LGBT travellers, and no government travel advisory flags trans-specific concerns.

Residual risks are minor: non-physical harassment (including online) is more common than violence but tends to be under-reported, and — in the unlikely event of arrest — prison practice has been found to lag the country's progressive law, with transgender inmates reporting gaps in healthcare and placement procedures.
MLT.outOfScopeNotes: Petty crime around nightclubs and tourist spots, and general European terrorism guidance, are ordinary travel risks that affect everyone.

ISL.name: Iceland
ISL.summary:
Iceland is one of the safest countries in the world for transgender visitors. The 2019 Gender Autonomy Act allows self-defined gender registration without diagnosis or surgery, non-binary people can use an "X" marker, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity and expression is banned in services and employment. General crime rates are very low.

Local travel businesses actively accommodate trans visitors: a dedicated traveller guide from Pink Iceland reports that most Reykjavík-area swimming pools offer private or gender-neutral changing rooms, that using binary changing rooms is legal and common, and that trans visitors generally "shouldn't have to be worried about your safety". Emergency services maintain dedicated guidance for queer victims of abuse and hate crime.

Residual risks are small: potential hate-crime reports have risen in recent years (from very low absolute levels), Iceland's hate-crime law works through sentencing aggravation rather than a standalone offence, and occasional misgendering — usually unintentional — still occurs.
ISL.outOfScopeNotes: Iceland's principal hazards are natural (weather, road conditions, geothermal and volcanic areas) and affect all travellers equally.

ESP.name: Spain
ESP.summary:
Spain is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. The 2023 "Trans Law" established legal gender recognition by self-identification and broad anti-discrimination protections, and a parallel penal-code reform made gender identity an explicit hate-crime ground — with real enforcement, including convictions carrying transphobia aggravation. There is no legal restriction on trans people using bathrooms or facilities matching their presentation, and the national tourism industry actively promotes Spain as an LGBTQ destination.

Acceptance is high in cities and tourist regions, though attitudes can be more conservative in some rural areas. Political debate around trans rights is heated, and some regional governments (Madrid, 2023) have rolled back regional protections — signals of a polarised climate rather than changes to a visitor's everyday legal position.

Documented incidents exist: harassment and verbal-abuse prosecutions, a high-profile local-police transphobia case in Benidorm, and gangs targeting queer tourists through dating apps (mainly gay men) in tourist zones — the latter being a general safety caution for app-based meetups anywhere.
ESP.outOfScopeNotes: Petty theft in tourist hotspots, drunken nightlife incidents, and general terrorism guidance affect all travellers. Dating-app meeting risks apply to everyone using them.

NLD.name: Netherlands
NLD.summary:
The Netherlands is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. Official guidance prepared for WorldPride Amsterdam 2026 confirms there are no visa or entry restrictions based on gender identity, passports with amended or "X" gender markers are accepted, and no medical documentation is needed. Discrimination based on gender identity is prohibited by law, and a 2025 law makes discriminatory motive an aggravating factor that can increase penalties by a third.

The country's institutions are strongly supportive: Amsterdam operates dedicated LGBTQIA+ reporting networks, and the mayor and police committed to priority investigation of Pride-period incidents in 2026. The capital is among Europe's safer cities for ordinary crime.

One caution: reported discrimination and violence against LGBTQ people has risen sharply since 2022 (anti-trans reports rose about 50% in the last year), and surveys indicate many queer residents avoid public displays of affection. For a visitor this translates mainly to a risk of harassment or verbal abuse, particularly late at night, rather than systematic danger.
NLD.outOfScopeNotes: Pickpocketing, bike theft, and taxi scams in Amsterdam affect all tourists.

USA.name: United States
USA.summary:
The United States has become a sharply split environment for transgender visitors, and the national score here reflects that average — see the Admin Divisions view for state-level scores, which range from among the world's most protective jurisdictions to states with criminal bathroom bans.

At the federal level, policy since January 2025 recognises only two sexes and no longer issues X or gender-affirmed passports (a policy the Supreme Court has allowed to remain in force). Foreign visitors with X or amended gender markers on their passports may face extra questioning or delays at the border, and several governments — including Denmark, Germany, Finland and the United Kingdom — have issued trans-specific travel advisories for the US. There is no verified reporting of a tourist being refused entry solely for being transgender, but documented cases of extended questioning exist, and border officers retain wide discretion.

State law varies enormously: roughly half of US states prohibit discrimination in public accommodations on gender identity, while around 22 states restrict transgender use of bathrooms and facilities — with criminal penalties in some (up to five years' imprisonment in Idaho, arrest-based enforcement in Florida, private "bounty" lawsuits in Kansas). Violence risk to visitors is low overall; the main concerns are legal exposure in restrictive states, document friction, and a hostile federal climate.
USA.outOfScopeNotes: Gun violence, mass-shooter risk, petty theft, and traffic safety are general US travel risks affecting everyone.

BRA.name: Brazil
BRA.summary:
Brazil combines some of the world's strongest legal protections for transgender people with a high level of real-world violence — the classic gap between law and practice. Courts allow name and gender-marker changes without surgery, the Supreme Court has criminalised transphobia (making it punishable like racism), courts fine businesses that discriminate, and official guidance affirms trans people's right to use bathrooms matching their identity.

For visitors, big-city queer life is vibrant and highly visible — São Paulo hosts the world's largest Pride parade — and the law is unambiguously on a trans traveller's side. The practical risks are concentrated in nightlife and app-based meetings: a majority of physical violence against LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo happens at night, and robbery schemes luring gay men via dating apps have been fatal.

Exercise particular caution after dark, with nightlife and app meetings, and in peripheral areas; general street crime — which affects all travellers — remains Brazil's main day-to-day hazard. Violence against local trans people (Brazil records the world's highest absolute toll) is heavily concentrated in poor and marginalised communities, not tourist areas.
BRA.outOfScopeNotes: Brazil's general crime problem (armed robbery, express kidnappings, gang violence) drives all governments to advise a high degree of caution for every traveller.

RUS.name: Russia
RUS.summary:
Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression — including, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and the US State Department explicitly warns LGBT travellers of this.

The UK Home Office assesses that trans people specifically are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution in Russia. Enforcement has produced over a hundred "extremism" convictions for displaying LGBT symbols or participation, bar raids, and the death in custody of a man who ran travel tours for gay customers. Enforcement focuses on public expression and activism rather than private existence, and same-sex activity itself is not criminalised — a discreet visitor is not automatically targeted — but there is effectively no police protection, and detention carries placement by passport sex.

Chechnya and the wider North Caucasus, where quasi-Sharia governance applies, are in a separate and graver category of danger for anyone perceived as LGBT.
RUS.outOfScopeNotes: The US State Department and most Western governments advise against all travel to Russia regardless of any personal characteristic, due to the risk of wrongful detention, the war in Ukraine, and arbitrary law enforcement.

SAU.name: Saudi Arabia
SAU.summary:
Saudi Arabia is among the most dangerous countries in the world for a transgender person to be discovered in. Under its uncodified Sharia legal system, same-sex conduct is punishable in theory by death, flogging, or long imprisonment, and transgender expression itself is criminalised through "imitation of the opposite sex" and public-morality provisions that police and the morality police enforce with broad discretion. There is no legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care is banned.

Enforcement is documented and brutal: trans women have been arrested, detained, and tortured on morality grounds; a Pakistani trans woman died in custody in Riyadh in 2017 after a raid; men have been arrested for cross-dressing videos posted online. Amnesty International reported in 2026 that visitors have been imprisoned after unfair trials over social media posts — including posts published before they entered the Kingdom — and device inspection at the border is an established risk.

The tourism authority's "everyone is welcome" messaging reflects official interest in visitors' money, not any change in law. Any practical safety depends entirely on never being discovered, including digitally; detention would be in facilities matching passport sex, with no consular leverage able to prevent mistreatment.
SAU.outOfScopeNotes: Missile and drone attacks on infrastructure, and the general risk of detention without charge for any visitor, affect all travellers.

AFG.name: Afghanistan
AFG.summary:
Afghanistan under the Taliban is the most hostile environment on this map for a transgender person. The 2024 Morality Law (PVPV) obliges the regime's virtue police to prevent "homosexuality" and "lesbianism"; the Taliban applies the death penalty for same-sex relations under its interpretation of Sharia; and documented practice against LGBTIQ people includes beatings, sexual violence in detention, forced confessions, and house-to-house searches. Transgender Afghans report living in hiding, in windowless rooms, for years.

There is no legal recognition, no protection, no functioning consular protection, and no tourism infrastructure that would allow a visitor to blend in. A discovered trans visitor would face the same enforcement apparatus as local LGBTIQ people: detention with routine sexual and physical abuse of queer detainees, prosecution for moral crimes, and corporal punishment that UN experts say is escalating into 2026.

This is the reference point for the very bottom of the risk scale.
AFG.outOfScopeNotes: Armed conflict, terrorism, kidnapping, and the arbitrary detention of foreign nationals for leverage are severe risks for every visitor to Afghanistan, independent of any personal characteristic.

GBR.name: United Kingdom
GBR.summary:
The United Kingdom has a documented, in-force rollback concentrated on facilities and detention that directly affects trans visitors. Bathroom and changing-room use is now directed by biological sex under the Equality watchdog's statutory code — a daily, nationwide civil restriction (the UK is the only country above 0.55 in this dataset with a nationally-legislated bathroom restriction). Since the April 2025 Supreme Court ruling, two severe-when-triggered risks apply if arrested: police forces strip-search trans women according to biological sex (with male officers), and trans women are placed in men's prisons — with documented suicide-risk litigation.

Documented trans killings have occurred (Brianna Ghey, 2023, and others). The climate is actively deteriorating via courts/EHRC-led rollback (not executive demonization — a contrast with the United States).

The UK's traveler-relevant positives are limited: no trans-specific border friction (foreign passports with X or amended markers are accepted), hate-crime law covering gender identity (theoretical recourse), no criminalisation, and functional institutions. The Gender Recognition Certificate and marriage equality — previously cited as positives — are resident-facing and do not apply to visitors.
GBR.outOfScopeNotes: Ordinary city crime in London and night-out alcohol incidents affect all travellers.

DEU.name: Germany
DEU.summary:
Germany is low-risk for transgender visitors, with two real caveats worth knowing. First, far-right street hostility is the most documented concern: roughly 110 of 245 Christopher Street Day (Pride) events in 2025 were disrupted or attacked, over half linked to organised far-right networks — a visitor at Pride, or visibly trans in the eastern Länder, faces elevated harassment. Second, if you are arrested, prison placement follows your self-chosen civil-registry gender entry under recent state-level reforms (better than France, which still places by legal gender/ID and has subjected trans women to gynaecological "verification"), but exceptions allow placement contrary to your self-declared gender and are invoked inconsistently — a neo-Nazi provocateur who self-ID'd to female was reassigned from a women's to a men's prison in 2026 after public outcry.

Offsetting this: bathrooms are unrestricted (venue-level sauna debates only), no border-police humiliation of trans travellers is documented, and carrying personal HRT through the Schengen area is uneventful. The Self-Determination Act (self-ID) is a positive climate signal though not itself a traveller-outing factor.
DEU.outOfScopeNotes: General urban crime is low; standard travel precautions suffice. The far-right street activity flagged affects Pride events and some eastern regions disproportionately.

JPN.name: Japan
JPN.summary:
Japan is a very safe destination for transgender visitors in practice, with a legal framework that lags behind. There is no national anti-discrimination law — the 2023 "understanding" law is symbolic — and legal gender change still requires a court process. But courts have moved in trans people's favour: the Supreme Court struck down the sterilisation requirement for legal gender change in 2023 and ruled workplace bathroom restrictions on a transgender woman illegal the same year.

Day-to-day risk is minimal: violent crime is rare, visibly trans visitors report curiosity more often than hostility, hotels and transport are unproblematic, and Tokyo and Osaka have an established queer scene. The main practical challenge is the strictly gendered, full-nudity culture of hot springs (onsen) — manageable using guides to gender-neutral or private rental baths and mixed open-air baths, which travellers actively share.

One caveat: online transphobic rhetoric and misinformation rose visibly during the 2023 legislative debates, indicating a live culture-war current, though it rarely translates into street-level trouble for visitors.
JPN.outOfScopeNotes: Natural disasters (earthquakes, typhoons) are Japan's principal travel risk and affect everyone.

THA.name: Thailand
THA.summary:
Thailand is one of Asia's most accepting destinations for transgender visitors. Visible gender variance is part of mainstream culture (the kathoey tradition long predates modern categories), the state actively promotes LGBTQ tourism, same-sex marriage became legal in January 2025 as the first in Southeast Asia, and the Immigration Bureau runs a dedicated "Welcome Pride" initiative to smooth entry for travellers whose passports don't match their appearance or gender. Gender-affirming healthcare is a mature, accessible industry.

The gaps are legal rather than social: there is still no procedure to change one's legal gender marker, the 2015 Gender Equality Act is weakly enforced, and — as the 2025 murder of a Thai trans woman in Pattaya highlighted — Thailand has no hate-crime law, so bias-motivated violence is prosecuted as ordinary crime.

For a visitor the practical risks are mostly Thailand's general ones: nightlife disputes, scams, and alcohol-fuelled incidents, with some reported friction in resort nightlife districts. Everyday movement, hotels, healthcare, and transit are unproblematic.
THA.outOfScopeNotes: Scams, drink-spiking in nightlife, road safety, and petty theft affect all travellers to Thailand.

MEX.name: Mexico
MEX.summary:
Mexico pairs meaningful legal progress with one of the world's highest tolls of violence against transgender people. Twenty-two of its 32 states offer administrative legal gender recognition, Mexico City and Nayarit have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections exist.

Against that, 71 trans or gender-diverse people were murdered in a single recent year — the second-highest figure in the Americas after Brazil — with organised crime increasingly involved and impunity near-total. The victims are overwhelmingly local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit, not tourists; violence is also highly concentrated by region.

In major tourist destinations and central Mexico City, heavily policed and progressively governed, a trans visitor's everyday risk is closer to harassment than violence. The dominant hazard for any traveller is Mexico's general crime environment. Use the Admin Divisions view: state-level scores range from among Latin America's best (Mexico City) to levels comparable with its most dangerous regions.
MEX.outOfScopeNotes: Cartel violence, kidnapping, and theft drive several governments to advise caution or non-essential travel avoidance for parts of Mexico — a risk independent of any personal characteristic.

BRN.name: Brunei
BRN.summary:
Brunei's Sharia Penal Code contains one of the world's most explicit trans-specific criminal provisions: Section 198 creates an offence of "a man posing as a woman or vice versa", and the Bruneian government has confirmed in its official guidance that the code applies to all persons in the country including tourists — travel agents are briefed accordingly. A separate indecency provision criminalises clothing that "tarnishes the image of Islam" with fines and imprisonment, and same-sex intimacy carries a stoning sentence (under a formal moratorium since 2019, with whipping and long prison terms actively available).

Enforcement is quiet rather than predatory — no prosecution of a foreign visitor under these provisions has been documented — but the country is an absolute monarchy with heavy surveillance, censorship, and no LGBT organising of any kind, and LGBT Bruneians have fled abroad. The legal exposure for a discovered trans visitor is categorical: no recognition, no protection, and gender expression itself is a written offence.
BRN.outOfScopeNotes: No current travel advisory flags general security risks; the hazards here are legal, not criminal.

PRT.name: Portugal
PRT.summary:
Portugal remains a low-risk destination for transgender visitors. The 2018 self-determination law allows legal gender and name change without medical requirements (minors 16-17 with parental consent), bathroom access matching one's gender is legally protected, conversion therapy is banned (2024), intersex infant surgery is banned, and hate-crime law covers gender identity — within an EU rule-of-law environment with very low violent crime. Same-sex marriage since 2010.

Two caveats pull it just below its Iberian neighbour Spain. First, in March 2026 the Portuguese parliament approved in first reading three bills (backed by the governing PSD/CDS and the far-right Chega) that would repeal the 2018 self-ID law, reintroduce a mandatory medical opinion, and ban hormones for minors. As of the most recent reporting this is not yet final law — it is in committee, and a government technical opinion warned it may be unconstitutional — so the self-ID framework is still in force. Second, hate-crime reports rose about 38% in both 2023 and 2024, with acknowledged under-reporting.

For a visitor these translate to a real political-hostility signal and elevated but still low-level harassment risk, not criminal exposure. The practical day-to-day environment is calm and welcoming, particularly in Lisbon and Porto.
PRT.outOfScopeNotes: Petty theft in tourist areas and a general terrorism guidance footnote affect all travellers.

IRL.name: Ireland
IRL.summary:
Ireland is a low-risk, calm destination for transgender visitors. It was one of the first countries in the world to introduce legal gender recognition by self-declaration — the Gender Recognition Act 2015 lets adults change their legal gender without medical requirements — and bathroom use is unrestricted. A hate-crime law covering sexual orientation and gender identity finally took effect at the end of 2024, equality law bans discrimination in employment, housing and services, and marriage equality was approved by referendum in 2015.

The caveats are stagnation and a mildly worsening climate rather than active rollback. The 2015 law is binary-only and long-promised reform (non-binary, under-16s) has stalled; transphobic hate speech remains uncriminalised after a 2024 government U-turn; a 2025 university study documented rising discrimination against sexual and gender minorities; and total hate-crime reports rose about 15% in 2025 (racism and xenophobia are the most common motives). None of this amounts to criminal exposure or physical danger for a visitor.

Day-to-day, Ireland is welcoming with low violent crime and a strong civil-society support network.
IRL.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory exists; general urban crime is low.

BEL.name: Belgium
BEL.summary:
Belgium is a top-tier, low-risk destination for transgender visitors. Legal gender and name change by self-declaration has been available since 2018 (with the constitutional reform that removed the former forced-divorce requirement), anti-discrimination law covers gender identity and expression across employment, housing and services, hate crime and hate speech are both criminalised for gender identity, and transphobia is a separately tracked hate-crime motive. Belgium also passed Europe's first femicide law (2023), with protections for gender minorities.

The framework is politically stable with no rollback movement — a contrast with several neighbours (the UK's in-force facilities code, Portugal's first-reading repeal attempt, Germany's repeal review). The main caveat is a documented rise in anti-LGBTQ violence and intimidation: the equality body Unia reported in 2025 that gay men and transgender people are increasingly targeted, and an RTBF investigation documented dating-app ambush attacks on queer men in urban nightlife.

For a visitor this is a low-risk environment with the usual urban-nightlife caution: zero legal exposure, functioning institutions, and a welcoming day-to-day climate, particularly in Brussels.
BEL.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; ordinary urban crime in Brussels affects all tourists.

FRA.name: France
FRA.summary:
France is low-risk for a transgender visitor, with risk concentrated on two specific situations. If you are arrested for any reason, including a protest or minor offence, a trans woman is likely to be placed in a men's prison on the basis of her legal gender — a systemic practice documented with foreign trans women (Argentine, Ecuadorian) subjected to genital-exam "verification," isolation and abuse. France's own detention watchdog says trans detainees "suffer the most," and a 2025 case (Louna, held in a men's prison in isolation) drew parliamentary censure.

At the border, trans women — especially racialised or Latin-American travellers — have been humiliated by French border police (the documented Giovanna case at Paris CDG), and the airport waiting-zones draw repeated discrimination criticism.

Offsetting this: there is no restriction on bathroom use, and the social norm leans trans-inclusive (a Lyon hostel in 2024 sanctioned a guest who complained about a trans person in a female dorm as "transphobic"). Anti-discrimination and hate-crime law cover gender identity. The risk is harassment-level in day-to-day tourism, with the serious-but-rare arrest/placement axis being the main caveat.
FRA.outOfScopeNotes: Urban crime (pickpocketing, theft) in Paris and Marseille, and the general risk of civil unrest/protests, affect all travellers.

CHE.name: Switzerland
CHE.summary:
Switzerland is a low-risk destination for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition has worked by self-declaration since January 2022 — a personal declaration before the civil registrar, with no court or medical requirements (binary male/female only; no non-binary marker). Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2022 (approved by referendum), gender-neutral rape law took effect in 2024, and employers have a legal duty of care toward trans employees. General crime is exceptionally low.

The notable legislative shortcoming — flagged by the ILGA Rainbow Map and by the government's own review — is that the criminal hate-crime and hate-speech provision (Article 261bis) covers sexual orientation but not gender identity. So a person targeted specifically for being trans does not benefit from that aggravation in criminal law, though the protections available through employment and constitutional law are broader. Reported hate crimes against LGBTIQ people have risen about fivefold since 2020 (around six per week, but from a low absolute base of ~309 cases in 2024).

The federal government adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against LGBTIQ hate crime in January 2026 (running to 2030), signalling a pro-trans institutional direction. There is no rollback movement.
CHE.outOfScopeNotes: Switzerland's principal travel risks (mountain/alpine hazards, road safety) affect all travellers.

AUT.name: Austria
AUT.summary:
Austria is a reduced-risk destination with a notably more conservative climate and a live far-right government hostility signal. The governing Freedom Party (FPÖ) mocks gender-diverse people publicly and has pledged a constitutional "two sexes" definition that would repeal non-binary protections — a threat, not yet enacted.

The most concrete traveler-relevant risk is organised dating-app predation: in 2025 authorities uncovered a neo-Nazi network that lured, beat, humiliated and filmed victims — primarily gay and bisexual men — through fake dating profiles (15 arrested). Caution is warranted on dating apps for queer travelers. There is no bathroom restriction law, no cross-dressing statute, and no documented border-police humiliation of trans travelers.

If detained, there are no specific legal protections for trans detainees — they are housed with the general population on an ad-hoc basis (only three trans people were in detention as of mid-2025). Trans-specific hate incidents actually declined in 2025, though homophobic violence rose. Legal gender recognition runs through the courts (the Constitutional Court affirmed gender identity as protected in December 2025).
AUT.outOfScopeNotes: General urban crime is low; the high cost of living is a non-safety travel note.

ITA.name: Italy
ITA.summary:
Italy is reduced-risk with several documented traveler-axis risks and a long-running government hostility climate. The most severe traveler-specific finding: two young transgender tourists were raped, and the convictions were confirmed on appeal in Naples in April 2026. Organised dating-app entrapment gangs have also been prosecuted (a Grindr-lure robbery gang in Padova; a 2025 assault in Bergamo).

There is documented police violence toward trans people: a Milan local-police officer was convicted in 2024 for beating a trans woman with batons in 2023. If arrested, trans women are placed in male prisons on the basis of biological sex (mitigated by a specialized section at Rome's Rebibbia prison). The Meloni government has run openly hostile rhetoric toward LGBT people for years — attacking the "LGBT lobby" and "gender ideology", and criminalising surrogacy abroad — and Italy is rated among the least progressive Western European countries on LGBT policy.

Major tourist cities (Rome, Milan, Florence) have established queer scenes and are generally safe day-to-day; bathrooms are unrestricted and there is no cross-dressing statute.
ITA.outOfScopeNotes: Pickpocketing and counterfeit-goods fines affect all tourists; no trans-specific travel advisory.

POL.name: Poland
POL.summary:
Poland is reduced-risk with two genuinely traveler-relevant weaknesses and a low-but-improving social baseline. In detention, Poland has documented severe failures involving foreign trans people directly: a Vietnamese trans woman was held in a male immigration-detention center with her hormone-therapy needs ignored, and the European Court of Human Rights found Poland violated a trans prisoner's rights by denying her HRT (2024). There is no specialized trans prison section analogous to Italy's Rebibbia.

Socially, the climate was deeply hostile under the previous Law and Justice government ("LGBT-free zones") and is improving under the Tusk coalition (a hate-speech reform draft in March 2025; ceased investigating foreign same-sex marriages), but a low baseline persists — Pride marches have been violently attacked (Białystok 2019), online anti-LGBT harassment is documented (Amnesty 2025), and rural areas draw harassment warnings. Legal gender recognition is court-based and medically gatekept, with no self-ID.

Bathrooms are unrestricted and there is no cross-dressing statute. Major cities are calmer than rural areas.
POL.outOfScopeNotes: Passport theft, unofficial-taxis overcharging, and general urban crime affect all travellers.

HUN.name: Hungary
HUN.summary:
Hungary is in a fast-improving post-Orbán transition. The most acute traveler-facing risk — the 2025 Pride ban with facial-recognition identification of attendees — has stopped: the 2026 Budapest Pride was held freely. Péter Magyar's Tisza party won a supermajority in April 2026, ending 16 years of Orbán rule, and the EU's top court has ruled that Hungary's 2021 "child protection" law breaches EU values (handing the new government a repeal mandate).

However, the Orbán-era laws remain on the books: a total ban on domestic legal gender recognition (2020), the "child protection" content law, and a constitutional amendment banning LGBTQ public events. The structural weakness that has not changed with the election is detention: a German court in 2025 blocked the extradition of a non-binary person to Hungary because of prison conditions and the person's identity, and watchdogs report transphobia in prisons with a "culture of silence."

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation of trans identity, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific entry friction. Social hostility lingers outside Budapest, but the state-led demonization that characterised the Orbán years has ended.
HUN.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is low.

GRC.name: Greece
GRC.summary:
Greece is a reduced-risk destination with a clear law-versus-practice gap. The legal framework is among Europe's strongest — it ranks 7th on the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map, has banned conversion therapy and intersex infant surgery, has a hate-crime law covering gender identity, and legalised same-sex marriage in 2024 (the first Orthodox-majority country to do so). There are no trans-specific border or bathroom restrictions, and the government is progressive with an improving trajectory.

But the social reality lags the law. A mob of about 150 people assaulted two trans people in Thessaloniki; an European Court of Human Rights case documented police detention and mistreatment of trans sex workers; surveys show Greeks are markedly more avoidant of public LGBTI visibility than the EU average (63% avoid holding hands); and the UK Foreign Office has issued an LGBTQ travel warning for Greece.

Major tourist destinations — Mykonos, Athens's Gazi district, Thessaloniki — are welcoming; outside them the climate is rougher than the law suggests.
GRC.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory beyond the UK Foreign Office's general LGBTQ note; ordinary tourist-season crime affects all travellers.

CZE.name: Czechia
CZE.summary:
Czechia is reduced-risk with an improving trajectory and a major welcoming tourist hub (Prague), offset by unprepared detention systems and elevated baseline social hostility. Legal gender recognition no longer requires surgery — the Constitutional Court struck that requirement in 2024 and the Health Ministry implemented reform in 2025 — but it still requires a medical diagnosis and 6–12 months' observation (improving, not self-ID).

If detained, the system is unprepared: the Supreme Court in November 2025 demanded prison rules for trans people, and there is a documented case of police mishandling the extradition-detention of an HIV-positive trans foreigner. About half of LGBTIQ people report being targeted by insults, assault or threats over five years, and the far-right SPD uses "deviant" rhetoric; Prague and larger cities are welcoming, but harassment is more likely in rural areas or late at night.

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation of trans identity, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction.
CZE.outOfScopeNotes: Pickpocketing and fake-plainclothes-police scams in Prague affect all tourists.

SVN.name: Slovenia
SVN.summary:
Slovenia is among Central and Eastern Europe's most progressive destinations for trans visitors, with a cleaner documented profile than its neighbours. Legal gender recognition is depathologised (no surgery or psychiatric-diagnosis requirement), and a 2022 reform abolished local jurisdiction in the gender-change procedure — reducing involuntary outing through local bureaucracy. Comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers gender identity, same-sex marriage is legal (2022, via the Constitutional Court), and no far-right party is in government.

No severe traveler-axis incidents surfaced in research: no mob violence against trans people, no trans-tourist rape, no European Court case of police abuse, and no documented foreign-trans-detention case — unlike several neighbours (Greece's Thessaloniki mob, Italy's tourist-rape and Milan police beating, Czechia's trans-foreigner extradition mishandling, Poland's foreign-trans-woman-in-male-detention). The main caveats are a far-right youth campaign ("Two Sexes, One Truth"), an underreporting/trust gap in hate-crime reporting, and thinner detention-placement evidence for a small country.
SVN.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is very low.

SRB.name: Serbia
SRB.summary:
Serbia is high-risk for trans visitors despite no criminalisation. The most acute documented traveler-axis risk is police: in February 2024 the Interior Ministry began investigating officers who beat, tortured and sexually harassed two LGBT people during a Belgrade apartment raid. About 105 sexual-orientation/gender-identity-motivated incidents were recorded in 2024, a masked attacker smashed the Pride information centre's front in 2025, Pride marches require heavy police protection, and testosterone HRT supply-chain disruptions have been documented.

Serbia is outside the Schengen area (border checks for foreign travellers), legal-gender-recognition reform has stalled (the Law on Gender Identity was not adopted), and the anti-discrimination law is weakly enforced — public institutions "make minimal effort." One mitigating factor is a Belgrade prison's trans-sensitive search policy, which lets trans women choose the search arrangement, though watchdogs flag training gaps.

Serbia has a lesbias prime minister (Ana Brnabić), but stalled legislation and police brutality make that largely symbolic rather than substantive protection. Major-tourist Belgrade is "conditionally" manageable with situational awareness.
SRB.outOfScopeNotes: General crime and border-corruption affect all travellers; Serbia is not a Schengen state so border checks apply to foreigners.

HRV.name: Croatia
HRV.summary:
Croatia is reduced-risk with a cleaner documented traveler-axis profile than its Balkan neighbours: no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, police-brutality case, or foreign-trans-detention case surfaced in research. The Dalmatian coast's international-tourism culture (Dubrovnik, Hvar, Split) is broadly open, and Zagreb has the Balkans' most established gay scene.

The framework is weaker than Western Europe's: legal gender recognition (available since 2015) is partial and not self-ID (it covers only some documents), there is no marriage equality (a 2013 constitutional ban), and an anti-gender movement is active. A 2024 prosecution of a host who refused to accommodate a gay couple shows enforcement works, and the President was formally criticised for outing a minister.

The Catholic-conservative climate is more marked outside the main tourist areas. Croatia is in the EU and Schengen, so border friction for most travellers is low.
HRV.outOfScopeNotes: General tourist-season crime and border checks for non-EU nationals affect all travellers.

EST.name: Estonia
EST.summary:
Estonia is reduced-risk with a strong progressive trajectory but a social climate that lags the law. It was the first Baltic and post-Soviet country to legalise same-sex marriage (2024), approved a national LGBT+ equal-opportunities action plan in 2025 (with particular attention to trans people), joined 16 EU states in urging Hungary to revise its anti-LGBT laws, and held Tallinn Pride in 2025. There are no documented severe traveler-axis incidents — no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, police-brutality, or foreign-trans-detention case.

The notable gap is legal gender recognition: it remains medical-gatekept (it requires a diagnosis and is "complicated, arbitrary"; a reform bill stalled), and surveys show Estonians are markedly more avoidant of public LGBTI visibility than the EU average (62% avoid holding hands; 40% avoid certain locations for fear of assault).

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction.
EST.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime very low.

LTU.name: Lithuania
LTU.summary:
Lithuania is reduced-risk, at the lower end, with one of Europe's most restrictive legal-gender-recognition situations. The Civil Code grants the right to medically change gender in principle, but there has been no legal framework regulating the procedure for 17 years — a deadlock the Constitutional Court refused to resolve in September 2025, perpetuating what an ECtHR body called a "distressing legal uncertainty."

Socially, a conservative climate is well documented: an MP called LGBT people "degenerated" and "spreading diseases" (his immunity was revoked), "traditional family values" groups disrupt peaceful protests, the Seimas Ombudsperson found police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to assembly, and trans people report systemic workplace harassment — open ridicule, isolation, and psychological abuse. A "Protection of Minors" law limits dissemination of LGBT information (a 2024 Constitutional Court ruling weakened its same-sex-family provision). There is no criminalisation, and LT Pride 2024 drew 15,000.
LTU.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; ordinary crime is low.

LVA.name: Latvia
LVA.summary:
Latvia is reduced-risk with no legal framework for gender recognition — trans people cannot legally change their gender marker, leaving those who've transitioned in a legal limbo. The most documented institutional failure is the European Court of Human Rights ruling Hanovs v. Latvia (2024), which found Latvia failed to prosecute a homophobic hate crime (the 2021 attack on lecturer Deniss Hanovs), violating the prohibition of inhuman treatment and the right to private life. There is no criminalisation, and bathrooms are unrestricted.

On the positive side, an administrative court overturned the denial of asylum to a Ghanaian LGBTI asylum-seeker in 2025, showing some institutional capacity for protection. The documented hostility is less extreme than in Lithuania (no "degenerate"-rhetoric MP, no propaganda-style minors law, no systemic-trans-workplace-harassment study surfaced), which places Latvia marginally above its southern neighbour.
LVA.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; ordinary crime is low.

TUR.name: Turkey
TUR.summary:
Turkey presents elevated risk for trans visitors — institutionalised, presidential-level hostility that has become state policy. Police profile and detain trans women for identity checks (20 were detained in Istanbul in July 2025), trans women have historically been "frequent targets of torture and ill-treatment" by police, and a trans woman attacked with a knife was herself detained (victim-criminalised). A draft law leaked in October 2025 would criminalise LGBT people — not yet passed but under active government consideration.

Transphobic attacks and Pride-event violence are documented, the Health Ministry is introducing regulations that may profile and restrict trans healthcare, and foreign visitors must carry original passports at all times — creating outing risk at the frequent transit checkpoints. If detained, trans women are placed in men's facilities with documented rights violations.

The risk is concentrated in urban trans-visible contexts (Istanbul's Beyoğlu/Tarlabaşı) rather than package-holiday tourist zones, but the institutional hostility pervades. Turkey is outside the Schengen area.
TUR.outOfScopeNotes: General terrorism and crime advisories affect all travellers to Turkey.

DNK.name: Denmark
DNK.summary:
Denmark is a low-risk, historically progressive destination. It was the first European country to introduce legal gender recognition by self-declaration (2014), has banned conversion therapy (2023), offers nonbinary gender markers, and has comprehensive anti-discrimination protections covering gender identity. There is no rollback movement, and Copenhagen ranks among the world's most LGBTQ+-welcoming cities.

One documented weakness: the Danish Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that a trans woman who legally changed her gender but hasn't had surgery must serve in a men's prison and be strip-searched by male staff — finding this did not violate the European Convention on Human Rights. This is the same prison-placement issue documented in France, Germany, and the UK. The Danish Institute for Human Rights also flags that police under-investigate hate crimes and are not obliged to flag hate-crime motivation at the time of reporting.

Anti-trans discourse is intensifying (debate over lowering the LGR age limit; an opinion piece by a former equality minister presenting trans people as a threat to gender equality) but has not produced rollback legislation.
DNK.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is low.

NOR.name: Norway
NOR.summary:
Norway is low-risk with strong legal protections and institutional responses, but a more acute violence context than its Nordic neighbours. Legal gender recognition by self-declaration since 2016; hate speech against trans people is criminalised (2020); anti-discrimination law covers gender identity; and the police operate a dedicated Hate Crime Unit with the security service providing annual Pride threat assessments.

The offsetting factors: a terrorist shot and killed two people at Oslo Pride in 2022 (the perpetrator, an ISIS sympathiser, was sentenced to 30 years); police-reported hate crimes against queer and trans people rose sharply in 2023 (up 18% overall, with trans-specific reports nearly doubling); an anti-gender movement is growing; and underreporting barriers are documented. The security service reports a significant decline in threats for 2025 Pride, but hate-speech and intimidation risks persist.

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction.
NOR.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory beyond its US travel update; general urban crime is very low.

SWE.name: Sweden
SWE.summary:
Sweden is low-risk. A new Legal Gender Recognition Act (July 2025) simplified the procedure and separated it from surgery requirements, but it still falls short of self-determination — a medical examination and a decision by the National Board of Health and Welfare are required. Sweden was the last Nordic country to reform its 1972-era LGR law.

One documented axis-C friction: the Medley swimming-pool company's national guidelines restrict trans persons' changing-room access — lawyers say this may violate discrimination law. Brå (the crime-prevention council) reports roughly 6,700 LGBTQI-related hate-crime reports, and the government is mapping digital threats against LGBTQI individuals. There are no documented severe incidents (no tourist-rape, mob violence, or Pride-terrorism equivalent to Norway's Oslo shooting). Bathrooms as such are unrestricted, and there is no criminalisation or rollback movement.
SWE.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is low.

FIN.name: Finland
FIN.summary:
Finland is low-risk. A 2023 reform removed the sterilisation requirement for legal gender recognition (Finland was the last EU country to do so), but a medical statement is still required — not full self-determination. Finland issued a US travel advisory for trans citizens in March 2025.

The Police University College reports record hate-crime levels (1,808 suspected cases in 2024, up 13% since 2023 — the majority racist, but sexual orientation is among the identified motives). There are no documented severe trans-specific incidents (no tourist-rape, mob violence, or police-brutality case). Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction.
FIN.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory beyond its US update; general urban crime is very low.

TWN.name: Taiwan
TWN.summary:
Taiwan is a progressive Asian destination — it was the first in Asia to legalise same-sex marriage (2019), the government is investing US$8.76 million to double gender-neutral public bathrooms by 2029, and a trans march in Taipei drew 3,000 participants in 2025. There are no documented severe incidents (no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, or organised dating-app predation).

The main gaps are legal-gender-recognition reform stagnation — a 2008 Ministry order still requires sex-reassignment surgery to change one's gender marker (blocking an estimated 90% of trans people, with only case-by-case court exceptions), and the government has been "floundering" on reform — and a rising anti-gender discourse movement that has produced online waves of hostility. A trans woman was outed during a police identity inspection (the Viva case), and Taipei has held a vigil for victims of anti-trans violence.

For a visitor, bathrooms are unrestricted (and being proactively expanded to gender-neutral), there is no criminalisation, and border/immigration poses no trans-specific friction. Taipei City has trans-friendly service guidelines.
TWN.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; earthquake/typhoon risks affect all travellers.

KOR.name: South Korea
KOR.summary:
South Korea is reduced-risk — there is no criminalisation, courts have protected trans people's restroom access and ruled favourably on legal gender recognition, and Seoul hosts one of Asia's largest Pride parades. But the country has no comprehensive anti-discrimination law (a gap not shared by EU peers), no same-sex marriage, and a conservative society where 67% of trans youth report hearing transphobic remarks from teachers.

Institutional friction is documented: the national human rights body flags a "transgender blind spot" in hospital wards (the Health Ministry can't answer how to accommodate trans patients); school bathrooms are a documented friction point for trans teens; and among trans people assigned male at birth who served in the mandatory military, 12% experienced sexual harassment or violence (this affects Korean conscripts, not foreign visitors). No severe incidents involving trans visitors are documented.

Legal gender recognition runs through the courts (surgery was historically required but courts are moving to allow changes without it). Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighborhoods are welcoming; outside them, more caution is warranted.
KOR.outOfScopeNotes: Foreign-tourist taxi scams and shopping complaints rose 71% in 2024 — general, not trans-specific.

IND.name: India
IND.summary:
India is elevated-risk for trans visitors, with a complex mix of constitutional protection and real practical gaps. The Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA judgment affirmed a constitutional right to self-determined gender identity, and the 2019 Act provides third-gender recognition. But a 2026 amendment bill — passed by parliament — has been called a "huge setback" by Human Rights Watch: it removes the self-identification right and narrows the legal definition.

Police abuse is documented (a trans woman was groped by a railway-protection constable to "check gender"; TheProbe documents police atrocities), airport security discriminated against a trans student at Chennai (CISF), passport authorities have demanded unwarranted medical exams, and a new penal code removed safeguards protecting trans people from sexual violence. Enforcement is uneven — only 11 of 36 states and territories have transgender protection cells.

India has no trans-murder toll comparable to Brazil and courts are protective, but the police abuse + amendment setback + safeguard removal + enforcement gaps + airport and passport friction place it in the Elevated-Risk band. Huge subnational variation is expected: liberal metros like Bangalore and Kerala are materially safer than conservative rural north and central states.
IND.outOfScopeNotes: General crime (theft, scams, sexual harassment of women tourists) is a documented concern in India affecting all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

CHN.name: China
CHN.summary:
China is elevated-risk — authoritarian but not criminalising. The most directly visitor-specific finding is airport discrimination: a Thai trans YouTuber was singled out and subjected to discriminatory treatment at a Chinese airport. The most severe documented case is forced psychiatric commitment: a trans woman was held for 97 days and subjected to electroshock "conversion" therapy under family pressure (she won unprecedented compensation), showing the medical/psychiatric system can be weaponized — though this targeted a resident, not a tourist.

Under Xi Jinping, the space for LGBTQ+ organising and expression is shrinking: Pride-month social-media and film censorship, a government crackdown on LGBT NGOs (2023), a performance ban on transgender TV icon Jin Xing, and cancellation of a foreign drag queen's tour. There is no criminalisation of trans identity, no bathroom restriction law, and courts can provide some protection, but there are no anti-discrimination protections and legal gender recognition requires surgery and parental consent at any age.

China is a regional gender-affirming-care hub, but the parental-consent barrier applies even to adults.
CHN.outOfScopeNotes: General state surveillance, internet censorship, and arbitrary-detention risks affect all travellers to China; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

MYS.name: Malaysia
MYS.summary:
Malaysia is high-risk — one of the few countries that criminalises gender expression per se. All 13 states and the Federal Territory prohibit "a man posing as a woman" under Sharia law (up to 3 years in jail, a fine, and caning). While these laws technically apply to Muslims, the enforcement climate affects all trans people: religious police conduct systematic raids on trans events — tipping off media in advance and sharing detainees' faces with tabloids (public outing and humiliation). Three trans women were killed in fewer than two months in 2019.

The political climate is shifting toward Islamist parties (a deputy minister urged the "deviant culture" label for LGBTQ; state-backed "rehabilitation" programs; dating-site blocking). For a non-Muslim foreign trans visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing law doesn't directly apply, but being caught in a raided venue, facing the enforcement climate, or being subject to Section 377A (same-sex conduct, 20 years + whipping, applies to all including tourists) are real risks. There is no legal gender recognition.
MYS.outOfScopeNotes: General crime and Islamic-law compliance (alcohol, dress codes for religious sites) affect Muslim and non-Muslim travellers in different ways; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

SGP.name: Singapore
SGP.summary:
Singapore is reduced-risk — far safer than its neighbour Malaysia, with no criminalisation of trans identity, no religious police, and one of the world's lowest crime rates. Section 377A (which criminalised sex between men) was repealed in 2022, and the prison service reports no assaults against its 10 transgender inmates — unusually positive for axis-H. Singapore is also a regional medical hub with gender-affirming care available.

The main gaps: legal gender recognition requires genital surgery (expensive and restrictive), there is no anti-discrimination law (the 2025 Workplace Fairness Act explicitly excludes sexual orientation and gender identity), and over 65% of trans Singaporeans report negative workplace experiences. A radio code still groups homosexuality with "paedophilia and incest" as lifestyles barred from the airwaves. Progress has "stalled" since the 377A repeal, with discrimination "quietly tolerated."

For a visitor: efficient border processing, very low street crime, unrestricted bathrooms, and no trans-specific police friction. The atmosphere is conservative but quietly accommodating in practice.
SGP.outOfScopeNotes: General crime is extremely low; no trans-specific travel advisory.

IRN.name: Iran
IRN.summary:
Iran is one of the world's most severe environments for trans people — but with a unique bifurcation. Same-sex conduct carries the death penalty, and a trans woman was raped in Ministry of Intelligence custody (the documented case of Ghazal Marzban in Evin Prison, 2023). The Tehran City Council ordered trans people to avoid "busy" areas of the capital. Trans people who have not had surgery face immorality and indecency provisions (imprisonment, fines, lashes) and documented forced-transition pressure — 6Rang describes "40 years of forcing gay people to choose between transitioning and death."

However, transsexuality IS legally recognised in Iran (under a 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Khomeini), and gender-affirming surgery is state-funded — making Iran one of the few countries in the region with any legal recognition of trans identity, and a trans medical-tourism hub. A post-operative trans visitor with matching documents is in a structurally different and better position than a pre-operative or non-binary visitor, or anyone perceived as same-sex-active — who face the death penalty, state-custody sexual violence, and forced-transition coercion.
IRN.outOfScopeNotes: General state-surveillance risks, compulsory hijab for all women, and the risk of arbitrary detention for foreign nationals affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

ISR.name: Israel
ISR.summary:
Israel is the Middle East's most progressive destination for trans visitors, with no criminalisation, anti-discrimination protections, court-based legal gender recognition (with dead-name removal from IDs as of 2025), publicly funded transition healthcare, and Tel Aviv as a regional queer hub.

Two traveler-specific risks pull the score down. First, Ben-Gurion Airport has no regulations for interacting with trans travelers — documented humiliating questioning and detainment, with surgery demanded for gender recognition ("If you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male"). Every foreign visitor transits Ben-Gurion, making this a high-probability friction point. Second, violence is rising sharply: 433 homophobic/transphobic physical incidents were reported in 2025, including dating-app traps and organized ambushes, with transgender people "bearing the brunt." Trump's anti-trans rhetoric is reportedly inflaming the local climate.

The right-wing Netanyahu coalition and the Israel-Hamas war aftermath have weakened protections, though the National Security Committee has convened on LGBTQ public-space security.
ISR.outOfScopeNotes: Security risks from the Israel-Hamas conflict (rockets, terrorism, border areas) affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

ARG.name: Argentina
ARG.summary:
Argentina has one of the world's most progressive legal frameworks — the 2012 Gender Identity Law allows administrative self-identification (no medical requirements), offers an X marker for non-binary people, funds transition healthcare, and same-sex marriage has been legal since 2010 (first in Latin America). Buenos Aires is "one of the safest major cities in Latin America for LGBTQ+ visitors."

But the situation is deteriorating sharply under the Milei government: the president has called "gender ideology" "child abuse," issued decrees modifying the Gender Identity Law (banning minors' hormone therapy and surgery; a prison-housing decree), and hate crimes hit a record 227 in 2025 (up 62%, one every 38 hours — trans women bearing the brunt). Police institutional violence against trans and travesti women is documented (arbitrary raids, drug-law criminalisation, searches only on travestis). The violence targets local vulnerable communities rather than tourists, but the trajectory is concerning.

The 2012 self-ID law remains in force for adults and courts are pushing back on the Milei decrees.
ARG.outOfScopeNotes: General crime (robbery, scams) in Buenos Aires affects all tourists; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

ARE.name: United Arab Emirates
ARE.summary:
The UAE is one of the most thoroughly documented trans-traveler-hostile countries in the world. At the border, trans visitors have been X-rayed to check their genitals (Israeli trans women, detained and denied entry at Dubai airport), deported for having a male passport (Thai model Rachaya Noppakaroon at Expo 2020; Gigi Gorgeous), denied entry despite valid UAE visas (Indian trans person), and sentenced to prison for "dressing in a feminine way" (Singaporean trans woman, 1 year in Abu Dhabi). A Brazilian trans woman was arrested in her Dubai apartment by plainclothes police accusing her of drug trafficking.

Same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 14 years). The state "employs various legal mechanisms to explicitly acknowledge and penalize nonconformity with traditional gender roles" and actively targets "non-Emirati tourists." There is no legal gender recognition.

However, the UAE does not have the death penalty for same-sex conduct (unlike Saudi Arabia or Iran), no documented custodial death of a trans person (unlike Saudi), and some trans visitors do enter successfully if their passport gender matches their presentation. The targeting is triggered by passport/presentation mismatch, not blanket.
ARE.outOfScopeNotes: Strict rules on social behaviour, drug possession, and financial crimes (exit bans) affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

ZAF.name: South Africa
ZAF.summary:
South Africa has one of the world's most progressive constitutional frameworks for trans rights — it was the first country to ban discrimination on sexual orientation (1996), has a legal gender recognition procedure (the Alteration of Sex Description Act, 2003), marriage equality (2006), and an Equality Act prohibiting unfair discrimination on gender. The Equality Court recently ruled in favour of a trans inmate who was denied gender expression and healthcare in prison (the Mokoena case, November 2025), affirming the constitutional right to gender-affirming healthcare for inmates, and Correctional Services has developed a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners.

But there is a wide gap between law and lived reality. LGR is administratively difficult, expensive, and inconsistently implemented ("the Mariana Trench of transphobia"). A trans woman was brutally attacked in a Tshwane tavern (January 2025); a Grindr-hostage ordeal was reported (December 2024); and anti-transgender violence has been documented within the public health system. There is a legal debate about whether businesses can refuse trans people facility access under the Consumer Protection Act.

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, private healthcare available, and Cape Town and Johannesburg have established queer scenes. The violence targets local trans communities, not tourists.
ZAF.outOfScopeNotes: South Africa's high general crime rate (violent crime, carjackings, muggings) affects all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

IDN.name: Indonesia
IDN.summary:
Indonesia is high-risk for trans visitors — with a directly documented trans-traveler death in custody and a presidential decree classifying LGBTQ+ as a national security threat. Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard trans activist from Peru, died in Bali police custody in 2022 after arrest at Bali airport on his honeymoon (family alleges police beating; police deny violence).

In Aceh province, Sharia law criminalises same-sex relations with public caning (applies to all persons in Aceh, including tourists). A new penal code effective January 2026 effectively criminalises all same-sex conduct nationally. President Prabowo in October 2025 classified "promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" as a national security threat alongside terrorism — and vigilante mob attacks on trans women escalated after this decree (10 attacks documented in Bogor between March and July 2026). Police conduct discriminatory raids on gay gatherings (75 arrested in Bogor in June 2025).

BUT: Bali is a major tourist hub where many trans visitors enter discreetly without incident; Indonesia has no death penalty; and Rodrigo's death is disputed (police deny violence) rather than clearly documented state torture.
IDN.outOfScopeNotes: Drug laws are severe (Rodrigo was arrested on drug charges); general terrorism/crime risks in certain regions affect all travellers.

PAK.name: Pakistan
PAK.summary:
Pakistan is high-risk — legally progressive on paper but severely undermined in practice. The 2018 Transgender Persons Protection Act was "one of the most progressive internationally" (third-gender recognition since 2009), but the Federal Shariat Court gutted it in 2023 (declaring provisions "un-Islamic"). Transgender people face extreme violence: three trans women were shot dead in Karachi (bodies on a roadside), 267 violence cases were documented in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and police commit a documented "continuum of violence — from routine harassment to arbitrary detention, extortion, and abuse in custody." The jirga (tribal) system closes cases under family pressure.

Same-sex conduct is NOT clearly criminalised nationally (the Zina Ordinance is unclear; no known cases or executions), and there is no Sharia cross-dressing criminalisation (unlike Malaysia). No trans-traveler-specific border friction or death in custody is documented (unlike the UAE or Indonesia). But the severity of social and police violence is extreme.

Pakistan has a significant hijra/third-gender community with some legal recognition, and civil society is active (a dedicated ride-sharing service for trans safety launched in Lahore, and activists are appealing the Shariat Court ruling to the Supreme Court).
PAK.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism risks, sectarian violence, and general crime in certain regions affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

PHL.name: Philippines
PHL.summary:
The Philippines is one of Asia's most socially accepting destinations for trans visitors, with deep cultural traditions of gender diversity (bakla, tomboy), a vibrant Manila Pride, and no criminalisation. Trans identity has never been criminalised.

However, there is a "near-complete absence of legal protections at the national level": no national legal gender recognition law at all (trans people cannot change their gender marker), the SOGIE Equality Bill has been stalled for 25 years (no national anti-discrimination law), and documented violence includes the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman found in a river (June 2025), a Chinese national arrested for raping a transwoman at a resort (May 2025), and a drag artist assaulted mid-performance. The Commission on Human Rights actively investigates discrimination cases but lacks enforcement power without a national law.

For a visitor: no border friction, social acceptance is genuine, but the legal-protection vacuum means limited recourse if discriminated against at a venue (documented incidents of bathroom, fitting-room, and resort denials).
PHL.outOfScopeNotes: General crime (kidnapping risks in certain provinces, scams, typhoon risks) affects all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

CHL.name: Chile
CHL.summary:
Chile has a strong legal framework — a gender identity law allowing self-determination (2019, no medical requirements), marriage equality (2022), a hate-crime law covering gender identity (2012), and a positive Gendarmería protocol that places trans inmates in facilities matching their gender identity and provides healthcare examination (better than most European countries on axis-H). The UN Human Rights Committee commended Chile's police measures to promote LGBTIQ rights.

But 2024 was a "year of regression" (the first rollback since democracy returned in 1990), with lawmakers rejecting nondiscrimination-law reforms and a 2025 Movilh report describing a "breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus" on LGBTIQ+ rights. Documented violence includes a trans person murdered and dismembered ("the biggest hate crime in Chile"), a transphobic hotel attack in Santiago (beating, captivity, death threats), and institutional discrimination against Chile's first trans police officer (relegated to admin, private life exposed, denied transition-surgery coverage).

The Supreme Court restored a femicide conviction for the murder of a trans woman (overturning an appeals-court ruling that she didn't "legally qualify" as a woman). For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms unrestricted, Santiago is welcoming.
CHL.outOfScopeNotes: General crime (theft, scams) and earthquake risk affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

COL.name: Colombia
COL.summary:
Colombia has one of Latin America's strongest legal frameworks — Constitutional Court legal gender recognition since 1993 (no surgery required, based on self-recognition), "trans" and "non-binary" ID markers (November 2025), a Comprehensive Trans Law being legislated (2025), marriage equality (2016), and a Constitutional Court ruling protecting a trans inmate from prison violence. President Petro's government is pro-LGBTIQ+.

But the law-versus-practice gap is extreme and violent. More than 40 trans women were killed in a single year, with armed groups running "social cleansing" campaigns (Caquetá) and posting kill-lists targeting specific LGBTQ individuals ("All will be military targets"). Sara Millerey, a trans woman, was tortured and murdered in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, with a viral video of the assault. The UN Independent Expert urged Colombia to "close the gap between laws and lived realities amid rising violence."

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, bathrooms unrestricted, Bogotá's Chapinero district is a well-established LGBTQ+ area. The armed-group violence is concentrated in conflict regions and targets local communities, not tourists — but the organized targeting is a distinctive, severe concern.
COL.outOfScopeNotes: The US State Department advises reconsidering travel to Colombia due to crime, terrorism, and kidnapping risks; these affect all travellers.

NGA.name: Nigeria
NGA.summary:
Nigeria is among the most severe environments for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the SSMPA (14 years, applies to all including tourists), and 12 northern states apply Sharia law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct. A transgender TikToker known as "Abuja Area Mama" was found beaten and dead on a highway in Abuja; police misgendered her in death and, six months later, no one has been arrested. Police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for "looking gay" — the SSMPA has been described as a "weaponised" law — and dating-app "kito" gangs use Grindr to lure victims into assault and robbery. The UK Foreign Office has warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks.

A proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public. Trans identity is NOT explicitly criminalized nationally (the SSMPA targets same-sex conduct), and the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists. But the Sharia death penalty, the trans-specific killing with impunity, the police brutality, and the UK advisory make this a Do Not Travel environment.
NGA.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism (Boko Haram in the northeast), kidnapping, and violent crime affect all travellers in many regions; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

KEN.name: Kenya
KEN.summary:
Kenya is high-risk for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the colonial-era Penal Code (14 years, applies to all including tourists). Police extortion targeting trans people is documented and systemic — a trans woman was forced to pay a $50 bribe in Mombasa, and 25 trans and intersex people told CNN this kind of police harassment is "common." The Kenya Human Rights Commission's "Lives on the Line" report documented 102 evictions, 43 unlawful arrests, and mob violence (groups stripping queer people naked) over a one-year period. An LGBTQ+ activist, Edwin Chiloba, was murdered (his body found in a metal box) — though the perpetrator was sentenced to 50 years, showing enforcement can work.

However, Kenya's courts have been a surprising bright spot. The High Court ruled in 2025 that a trans woman's arrest for "personation" was unconstitutional (awarding damages and ordering the government to draft a Transgender Protection Rights Bill). In May 2026, the High Court affirmed a constitutional right to legal gender recognition. The Supreme Court has upheld LGBTQ+ freedom of association, and the Court of Appeal ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional. "Thousands of gay travelers visit annually through specialized tour operators."

There is no anti-discrimination law and no LGR procedure yet, but the court-ordered Transgender Protection Rights Bill is a positive trajectory.
KEN.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism risks near the Somali border, general crime, and political instability affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

ROU.name: Romania
ROU.summary:
Romania is reduced-risk with a conservative political climate and significant legal-protection gaps, but a landmark EU court ruling and active civil society provide some positive trajectory. The European Court of Justice ruled in 2024 that Romania must recognize gender-identity changes made in other EU member states (the Mirin case), and a Romanian court definitively confirmed this in March 2026. Bucharest Pride marked its 20th anniversary with tens of thousands of marchers.

However, domestic legal gender recognition is court-based, restrictive, and inconsistently implemented. The anti-discrimination law does not explicitly cover gender identity (it covers "sex" and "sexual orientation" only), and the hate-crime law's aggravating-circumstance provision has never been applied in SOGIESC cases. No same-sex marriage or civil unions are recognised (the Orthodox Church successfully opposed reform). Far-right influences rose during the 2024-2025 election cycle, with anti-LGBTI rhetoric "intensified and repeatedly instrumentalised for political mobilisation."

For a visitor: EU/Schengen, no trans-specific border friction, no criminalisation, bathrooms unrestricted. The ECJ ruling means EU-issued LGR documents must be recognised.
ROU.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is moderate.

BGD.name: Bangladesh
BGD.summary:
Bangladesh is high-risk for trans visitors, with escalating Islamist violence since the August 2024 political crisis that ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. Trans activist Shila was brutally murdered in February 2025 (police suspect extremist involvement). A human-rights group documented 260 anti-LGBTQI+ incidents in 2024 — including murder, arson, and blackmail — describing attacks as having "skyrocketed." Islamist fundamentalist groups have intensified attacks under the interim government, and LGBTQ+ people have been "forced into hiding." A mob stormed the gate of a safe house for third-gender people (one survivor said "I escaped only with my life").

Same-sex conduct is criminalised under colonial-era Section 377 (life imprisonment, "rarely enforced" but used by police for harassment and extortion). Hijra people are legally recognised as a third gender (2013/2014, a genuine positive), but there is no anti-discrimination law and no comprehensive legal gender recognition. Police extort hijra/trans people — dozens were arrested for refusing to pay extortion money, and five were arrested at Dhaka's international airport.

The US State Department rates Bangladesh as Level 3 (Reconsider Travel).
BGD.outOfScopeNotes: Political instability, mob violence/lynchings, terrorism, and cyclone/monsoon risks affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

VNM.name: Vietnam
VNM.summary:
Vietnam is reduced-risk — described as "one of Asia's most tolerant countries toward sexual minorities." Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the Civil Code (2015, Article 37) was a landmark that recognised transgender people's right to change their legal gender. However, the implementing Gender Affirmation Law has been stalled for over eight years — the right exists on paper but not in practice. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity.

No trans-specific killing has been documented (unlike several neighbours), but conversion efforts (SOGICE) are documented, and healthcare discrimination is a significant barrier — trans people face stigma, lack of trans-competent providers, and "red tape" in accessing care. In September 2025, Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and five LGBTQ events, shocking activists (though Hanoi's Pride proceeded).

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, bathrooms unrestricted, and no criminalisation. But Vietnam is a one-party authoritarian state where "rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice" (Amnesty), and the stalled LGR means no practical gender-marker change. The UN Development Programme is actively engaged on trans-rights strategies.
VNM.outOfScopeNotes: One-party state political controls, arbitrary detention of dissidents, and typhoon/monsoon risks affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

UGA.name: Uganda
UGA.summary:
Uganda is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. The 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act imposes life imprisonment for same-sex conduct and the death penalty for "aggravated homosexuality," and the US State Department explicitly warns that "the law applies to both visitors and residents." Over 1,000 rights violations (arrests, torture, evictions) were documented in nine months. Mobs have gathered outside trans people's homes (one woman described being grabbed and shouted at that she needed to die); police use digital entrapment (obtaining evidence via dating apps); and the government has "spread misinformation and hatred against LGBT people." The law also criminalises the "promotion of homosexuality," meaning any advocacy or support is banned.

There are no laws regulating gender identity — the AHA targets same-sex conduct and promotion, not trans identity per se — but trans people are swept up in the broader anti-LGBT crackdown, mobs, and state violence. The Constitutional Court upheld the AHA in April 2024 (striking down only a few provisions on healthcare access and renting).

Uganda's death penalty is for "aggravated" same-sex (not all same-sex like Iran; not gender expression per se like Saudi), and no trans-specific visitor killing or border-targeting is documented — but the systematic state-led crackdown makes this a Do Not Travel environment.
UGA.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism (ADF in border areas), violent crime (armed robbery, sexual assault), and civil unrest affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

EGY.name: Egypt
EGY.summary:
Egypt is high-risk for trans visitors — with a directly documented study on the treatment of queer foreigners by Egyptian authorities ("Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here," Cairo 52, 12 incidents 2018-2022). Same-sex conduct is not explicitly criminalised, but authorities use "debauchery" and cybercrime laws (six months + fine for "violation of social and family values") to arrest and prosecute — and courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation under the cybercrime law.

Police hunt LGBT people on dating apps (BBC Grindr entrapment) and subject arrestees to coerced anal examinations. Gender-affirming healthcare is prohibited. The Ministry of Interior is closing a loophole that allowed limited legal gender recognition. Egypt rejected all UN recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity in its 2025 Universal Periodic Review. The authorities' approach is described as "not only to criminalize LGBTQ+ identities but also to erase them from society and public life."
